utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic is continuing his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Jokanovic.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript could we please clarify a few things. After the vote was held concerning the amendments to the Serbian constitution, did the Kosovo Assembly resume its work?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a 20-minute break after which the Assembly continued working in Chambers. An introductory address was then done by Mr. Susuri who was the deputy prime minister of the Kosovo government. The Yugoslav programme on the prevention of people immigrating from Kosovo and returning those who had immigrated to come back was considered, as well as the issue of appointments and elections. A number of judges and court presidents were elected as well as prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that after the Assembly held on the 23rd of March, 1998, there was a European parliament delegation which came to visit who comprised the delegation and who received it?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the European parliament delegation. Whether they met with anyone from the official institutions in addition to meeting me, that is something I don't know. I do think their intention was to visit only the speaker of the Assembly. I held talks with them, they were fruitful. I explained the situation in Kosovo and discussed with them the provincial Assembly session in question as well as the contents of the amendments that were carried a few days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P286.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that is coming up, Mr. Djurdjic, line 19 of page 1, I don't think we have the correct name of the deputy prime minister of the Kosovo government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, can you slowly tell us the first and last name of the vice-president of the executive Chamber or council of Kosovo Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the vice-president of the Executive Council of Kosovo Hazir Susuri with two Ss. Do I need to repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, that's fine. Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Jokanovic, on the screen we have the transcript of a statement by Mr. Rugova, which he gave, actually this is his testimony in the case against Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to the 3rd of May, 2002, page 4191.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: There's no need for you to try to find what I'm looking for. I'll read out to you what Mr. Rugova said in his answer. Lines 4 to 12 Mr. Rugova states: "Yes, the Kosovo Assembly was supposed to discuss the suspension of the federal status of Kosova inside the Federation and its autonomous status. Great pressure was brought to bear on the deputies of the parliament to vote in favour of that measure, but the public was against, that is to say, the citizens and people at large. Pressure and violence was used. I remember there were tanks surrounding the parliament building. In the parliament building itself, there were police, secret police dressed in civilian clothes. Therefore, the members had to vote under pressure. Some members did vote." Mr. Jokanovic, there is a number of issues contained in this answer. I would like to break them down. First of all, did the Kosovo Assembly discuss the suspension of the status of Kosovo within the Federation?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kosova Assembly did not discuss such suspension of Kosovo within the Federation. It could not have because the position of the province was prescribed under the SFRY constitution. These amendments did not go to change the status of province within the Federation itself. It is contained within the amendments themselves, amendments 9 through to 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any tanks around the parliamentary building of Kosova during the session?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no tanks around the parliament building. There was also a statement to the effect that there were armoured vehicles. There were none of those either. The situation was quite calm around the Assembly building. There were 180 journalists and reporters, representatives and guests from all over the country. No one, however, took note of that. No one published that fact. No paper in Yugoslavia or in the world carried that. As for the tanks and armoured vehicles and the police inside the building, this is something I heard only as late as 1986 when Baton Haxhiu he was a witness here, I believe, I'll recall his last name later. He interviewed me for the "Koha" newspaper. He put that very question to me. "Koha" translated into Serbo-Croatian means time. Baton Haxhiu. I gave him that interview and I basically said everything I'm telling you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next Mr. Rugova says that there were secret police in the building dressed in civilian clothes and that because of that, the Assembly deputy said to vote under pressure. Were there any pressures exerted, Mr. Jokanovic?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly, much as any other Assembly in the world, had its security service at the entrance. No one could enter the building unless they were invited or working in the building, or if they had not been accredited as journalists. As for any secret police, that's something I'm not aware of. I would have known had there been any. Any deputy or at least one of the them would have mentioned that for sure. They were not in the Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page, lines 14 to 16, Mr. Rugova states: "I remember ten members voting against it. Then these members were sentenced, punished somewhere, sent to prison somewhere." Mr. Jokanovic, was anyone sentenced because of voting against the changes out of the representatives there and deputies?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the Assembly as in any other Assembly enjoy immunity. They cannot be prosecuted unless their immunity is revoked by the Assembly itself. So the delegates who voted against could not have been arrested or prosecuted in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that at a later point there were also some amendments carried concerning the provincial constitution. When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-1989, say in June or July. I can't recall exactly. This happened based on the amendments to the Serbian constitution. Before that, there had also been amendment made to the federal constitution. Those amendments had to do with certain economic issues as well as issues of self-governing of associated labour, as we called it at the time. It was necessary to carry out this harmonisation exercise between the Kosovo constitution with the constitutions of Serbia and the federal constitution. So during the session in June or July, those amendments were carried to the Kosovo constitution. I explained the gist of those constitutions after which there was a vote. They were carried unanimously. There were no issues surrounding the whole thing because the provincial status was preserved within the Federation, i.e., that the province was a constituent part of Serbia and the Federation, which had been the bedrock of the constitutions -- of the constitution of the 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: During the session in June, were there any delegates against the amendments made to the Serbian constitution which took place in March?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall them individually, but the Assembly comprised the same members. I can't tell you exactly who was present because it's been a long time, and I couldn't definitely recall every person's name. I presume they were there although some of them may have been absent. In any case, there was sufficient two-third majority at the Assembly which were in favour of the amendments to the constitution of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, until which time the provincial Assembly worked in that composition?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly worked in that composition until December. In December new elections were scheduled in Kosovo and in the Republic of Serbia. All of the citizens participated in those elections and the response of the voters was quite large. The deputies were elected for the new Assembly in those elections as well as the members of the Serbian Assembly following which all organs and all bodies was established both in the province and in the Federation which is to say that Djordje Bozovic was elected speaker of the Kosovo Assembly. Kamdonce [phoen], was president of the Presidency, and other officials were appointed to various offices, to the crisis council and so on. All other organs were established within the province.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us in which year these elections were held?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the political situation was like in the SFRY after those general elections and throughout 1990?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990 the political situation in Yugoslavia was quite unfavourable. The relations deteriorated and the situation was quite unfavourable in view of the prospective and the survival of Yugoslavia. I don't remember exactly the date, but during that period of time, from the central committee of the legal communists of Yugoslavia, the delegates of Slovenia walked out. They left that body, following which the delegates from Croatia left that body too. So that the league of communists was significantly weakened, and this heralded the disintegration of Yugoslavia. While Tito was alive he was the factor that preserved the unity of Yugoslavia, but after his death the key element at preserving the unity of Yugoslavia was the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and once the League of Communists of Yugoslavia started disintegrating, this heralded the falling apart of Yugoslavia which in its turn caused the situation in the entire country to be very unfavourable and difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Following those elections, who was the president of the Presidency of Kosovo and also who was the president -- chairman of the League of Communists in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that year it was Rrahman Morina who was the chairman of the League of Communists. Prior to him it was Azem Vllasi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the president of the Executive Council which was the government?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Executive Council in the previous composition was Nazim Mustafa and after that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How did the events in SFRY that you just described effect the situation in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events in Yugoslavia at the beginning of disintegration of the League of Communists as the element that kept the country together directly affected the situation in Kosovo since it became evident that the disintegration of Yugoslavia was imminent and that referendums were being prepared in Slovenia and also other events which transpired later on in Kosovo the political parties that were established, the democratic Alliance of Kosovo and also other political parties that were registered and also those that were not registered, all of them started working quite actively. They saw their chance in the disintegration of Yugoslavia. They saw that they could attain their separatist goals of separating Kosovo from Serbia and Yugoslavia. This is why they copied the conduct and the event of people in Slovenia and later on in Croatia. But to make it clear, unlike Slovenia and to some extent Croatia, there was a major constitutional hindrance that prevented Kosovo from becoming independent. Kosovo was not a republic, and Albanians, according to the constitution, were not a nation but a nationality. Whereas the constitution of Yugoslavia guaranteed self-determination and cessation only to the republics and only to nations, and this province did not have that right under the constitution. This is why a separatist activity was being conducted in Kosovo which grew into a separatist nationalist movement aimed at giving an identical status to Kosovo even if it was unconstitutional but granting it the status of a republic so that they could use it in order to achieve their goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how did the events in Kosovo and Metohija unfold following that, according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-1990 this newly elected Assembly due to all of these events in Yugoslavia and due to an open separatism that emerged in Yugoslavia, the problems in Kosovo emerged and became more tense. I could tell you about the problems that I was most familiar with, and those were problems in the provincial Assembly. It was head by Bosa Djordjevic, and the Assembly had major difficulties in work, the work could not transpire in a normal atmosphere. Rather there were frequent chaotic situations, people pushing each other away from the speaking podium and having major conflicts in the work -- in the session of the Assembly among the delegates. Something that a president of the Assembly Djordje Bozovic frequently mentioned was that Albanian delegates wanted to read the declaration on independence of Kosovo at the Assembly session and then suspended work of the session. Djordje Bozovic and other delegates disagreed with that, and the work of the Assembly was discontinued because it couldn't continue normally, and it couldn't continue in a normal atmosphere where delegates would take the floor in a normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: After the work of the Assembly was disrupted, what happened afterwards --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not objecting, and I have no problems with the witness answering the question. It's just that the witness in the introductory part of his testimony yesterday indicated that he had been elected to a position outside of Kosovo by the latter part of 1989. So, therefore, in 1990 and thereafter he would be involved in work outside of Kosovo. Not that the evidence is not admissible, but the usual practice is that if it is going to be hearsay, he should at least give the basis for his information, the basis for the evidence that he is giving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, I think you followed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me? I think that the witness is about to lay the foundation as to where he gained the knowledge about what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not a matter of thinking. You should ensure that he first has done so. If you could achieve that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I were to give an explanation, then I would be testifying, and we have a witness here in the witness box so this is why I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your questions must lay the foundation and then the relevant evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, in mid-1990 what office did you hold?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Belgrade. I was deputy president of the Assembly of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As deputy president of the Assembly of Serbia, did you have contact with the president of the Kosovo Assembly and with the delegates in the Kosovo Assembly, and if so, describe those contacts to us?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mostly was in contact with the president of the Kosovo Assembly, Djordje Bozovic. I had official contacts with him via telephone and in personal contact, and I also had contacts with other delegates on various occasions, but mostly with the president, Djordje Bozovic. Since I was from Kosovo, when it came to any major problems and issues, they would inform me. He, Djordje Bozovic, would inform the president of the Serbian Assembly but also me. And then the president of the Serbian Assembly given the fact that I was from Kosovo would also inform me about what he had learned from Djordje Bozovic and about the work of the Kosovo Assembly. So the prosecutor is quite right, I was indeed in Belgrade, and I wasn't directly personally present, however, the source of the information I received was the president of the Kosovo Assembly and also on some occasions president of the Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings where president of the Kosovo Assembly was also present in mid-1990 and if so, what happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Djordje Bozovic, president of the Kosovo Assembly, came to Belgrade to a meeting with a large group of delegates of the Kosovo Assembly, a meeting with the president of the Serbian Assembly and other political leaders in Serbia to voice the problems he was encountering and proposals as to what needs to be done. A meeting was held in Belgrade. I was asked to attend that meeting by the then-president of the Serbian Assembly Zoran Sokolovic, and I did come to that meeting as did other officials of Serbia. Djordje Bozovic and the delegates from Kosovo informed us that they were unable to continue working normally, that the Assembly was faced with a situation where any normal work was no longer possible and they didn't want to continue with their Assembly session in Pristina. They didn't want to go back to Pristina. After long talks and efforts to convince them, delegates did return to Pristina and continued the work of the provincial Assembly, but it didn't last for a long time. Once they resumed their work, they worked only briefly because Dr. Stanoje Dogandzic, a university professor, took the floor and on behalf of some delegates, he spoke saying that the Assembly did not have the necessary conditions for normal work, and he asked the president of the Assembly to officially address the authorities so that the Assembly discontinued its work. There were some commotion, from what I could understand, and once again the Assembly was suspended. And then a request was sent to the Serbian Assembly to temporarily dismiss the Assembly of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how did the Serbian Assembly react to this proposal?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly scheduled sessions of all three Chambers and adopted the law on dissolving the provincial Assembly which said that until the new Assembly was re-established, the republic Assembly would continue the work of the provincial Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what was the reaction of the Albanian delegates in the Kosovo Assembly after the Assembly was dissolved?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the information that Djordje Bozovic had and that he conveyed to me, and given that there was an effort to read the declaration at the session of the Assembly, when the Assembly was dissolved, a number of delegates assembled in front of the Assembly building. One of those who was present came from the circle of public figures and renowned figures. I think he was from the provincial theatre, and he read the declaration according to which Kosovo was independent and Kosovo was declared to be a state. There was a TV crew that recorded that and the reading of that declaration took place right next to the building of the provincial Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, when did this take place, this reading of the declaration in front of the provincial Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1990 when Yugoslavia started falling apart, when tensions escalated, when the work of the Assembly of the province became quite difficult, and when other organs could no longer function.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the month when that took place?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was either in June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the session when the amendments to the constitution of the Republic of Serbia were approved, when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of March, 1989, which is to say, some 18 months prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jokanovic, what was the nature of your relationship with the Albanians that you worked and lived with in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in Kosovo. I completed my elementary and secondary school in Kosovo. For most of my work life I worked in Kosovo until the year 1990, so my relation with the Albanians, the Turks, and members of other nationalities and obviously with the Serbs, were very good. They did not only involve our common work, are our common political activity but also we used to spend time socially, privately, and we would visit one another's homes. We celebrated together different weddings and other festivities, so generally speaking, I had very good relations with Albanians. I had many friends who were Albanians and Turks. I also have such friends today. Unfortunately some of those Albanian friends are my former friends, I certainly hope they will be my future friends as well. Some of them are also coming to see me in Belgrade, we visit regularly and we discuss the current issues in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, you told us that you were from the village of Grmovo. Could you tell us in your village what was the ethnic composition of the population there?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in Gornje Slatina because my father who was a teacher at the time worked in that village, and his native village and my native village was Grmovo was the adjacent village to Gornje Slatina. So in Grmovo, I had a family house, and this is the village that I considered to be my home village. You asked me about the ethnic composition of Grmovo. In my village of Grmovo the ethnic composition changed as it did everywhere else in Kosovo, so in 1960s there were more than 70 houses that belonged to Serbs and Montenegrins, and some 15 that belonged to Albanians. Later on, the number of houses as well as the population was reduced, and before the NATO bombing, we had some 30 plus Montenegrin and Serbian houses and over 100 Albanian houses. Out of the population of some 550 or 600, who were Serbs, that number was reduced to approximately 150. So the ethnic composition changed, the Albanians are nowadays a majority, and the number of Albanian households also forms a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you still have a family house in your home village?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kosovo and in my home village, I still have some property, but the house that I used to have there, after I first came were first of all destroyed and later on burnt down, so no Serbian or Roma house remained there. The church was also mined and the graveyard was desecrated. My house in Grmovo there was an attempt by some Albanian neighbours to prevent the burning of my house. However, they were unable to do that, and they could not resist armed people who came there, so I later on received some pictures of my house that were sent to me by a friend of mine, an Albanian, immediately after it was pulled down. So I still have some property in Kosovo. I have some land that I inherited, but I still cannot do anything with that land as its rightful owner due to the problems in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the document D006-4467.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, could you please tell me what is it that you can see on these three pictures that are on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first photo is a small house in a village built in a typical style of that village and this is what it used look like, and the remaining pictures are what you could see after KFOR came to Kosovo. So I remained without my home house, without my place of birth, which obviously has spiritual repercussions for any person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Another thing, what is the ethnic composition of the population of your village of Grmovo right now?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately in my village of Grmovo there isn't anybody of either Serbian, Roma, or any other nationality there nowadays. The houses that were destroyed are still destroyed. As you can see on these pictures, and they haven't been repaired, and I would like my house to be repaired that I hope that the last years of my life I will be able to spend there again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jokanovic, for your testimony. Your Honours, with this I have completed my questions. Could we just please tender these pictures into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00909.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Mr. Stamp is is getting organised. When you are ready, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jokanovic.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall saying at any time that the 1974 constitution of the SFRY constituted a grave injustice to the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can recall the statements of that time. Many people were saying that in Serbia and in Yugoslavia. There were a number of documents which pointed to this fact. I spoke about a Blue Book when I was asked by the counsel. I also mentioned other discussions, and the conclusions of the highest bodies of the Yugoslav League of Communists also talked about an inadequate position of Serbia in comparison to other republics. What I didn't say was that some of the university teachers and intellectuals were politically persecuted, and Professor Djuric was imprisoned for one year because he resisted that constitution which put Serbia into an unequal position. So I also recall myself saying similar things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It was your view, was it not, that it gave Kosovo too much autonomy and it left the Serbs living in Kosovo vulnerable to discrimination by a government of Kosovo that was dominated by Albanians?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a public personality, as a politician, I gave a number of statements and I gave certainly statements to that effect. And they were truthful. And the position of Kosovo pursuant to the 1974 constitution nearly put Kosovo at the same level as republics, and Serbia was divided in three parts. So this was that unfavourable position which furthermore influenced the position of Serbs and Montenegrins who then started to move out from Kosovo. So maybe I didn't use those same words, but I made statements to the same effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were shown a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring it up again, it's D905.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a conclusion of the SFRY Assembly on the 3rd of March, 1989. This was a conclusion, is that it? Yes. Now, in accordance with these conclusions, did the federal authority, that is the SFRY authorities, assume responsibility for police security within Kosovo as a part of special measures to be implemented for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the different bodies in the Federation at the level of the republic and at the level of the province, so in line with these conclusions they are different tasks for the organs of the republic and organs of the province. They are all stipulated clearly item by item, obviously we can read them all out, and particular items are very significant in view of the minor strike that we had prior to this. So the federal Assembly stated that it was inadmissible for the functioners to be replaced or dismissed away from the institutions of the system. Also it calls for criminal responsibility of persons who committed such acts and so on and so on. In line with these conclusions, the federal executive committee also passed a number of conclusions whereby they wanted to put these conclusions into practice, and prior to these conclusions, there was a decision of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to introduce special measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. And among the special measures introduced was that the SFRY authorities would assume responsibility for police security within Kosovo. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If possible, if you could assist me with this. I would like to know which particular item of the conclusions you are pointing to. 23

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only tell you that this is number 5 in your binder and maybe Mr. Stamp can help you with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not pointing you to a particular provision in those conclusions. I'm asking, I'm suggesting that the conclusions taken as a whole resulted in the federal SFRY authorities assuming control of the security situation in Kosovo. Is that your memory?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't recall that they didn't fully assume the authority for the security in the territory of Kosovo because in the territory of Kosovo there were the relevant bodies there. There was the Executive Council and also there were police units there, so there were also security organs there, so they carried out their responsibilities pursuant to the constitution and the law. And those also listed in the items of these conclusions. And you could not act outside of what was stipulated in these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the special circumstances and special measures discussed in those conclusions, were these eventually set out in decisions of the Serbian authorities? Or perhaps I could show you the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P71 quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is the 26th of June 1990. Do you recall this decision?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a decision, I can't read this very clearly, decision on special circumstances in the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo. Yes, this decision was probably made in line with the previous conclusions, and indeed Zoran Sokolovic was president of the Assembly at the time and the presidents of the chambers listed down here were indeed presidents of the chambers at the time. And indeed we did have special circumstances at the time, which was the result of the decision made by the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could look at P496. We have to go to page 2 for the translation. That's page 2 of the document on the right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just tell us firstly from your copy what is the date of this law?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the date. It was in June. I believe it might have been 30th. I think it was June the 30th. No, no, it's not the 26th or the 28th. I'm not sure. The 26th it seems. June 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do you recall the previous decision, and this law had the effect of enabling the SFRY authorities to take control of the security responsibilities in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This law is related to the previous decision by which it was established that special circumstances were in place. Based on that Assembly decision, this law was promulgated on how the authorities were to act under such circumstances. However, this is a republican law speaking of the republican organs, bodies in Serbia. It is based on these conclusions and special circumstance that the provincial organs also pronounced their own measures arising from the conclusions of the federal Assembly during the period of time when they were operational. The conclusions were dated the 3rd of March, 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. And I just show you these documents hoping that you may remember, if you do, that part of a special measures involved the take-over of the security apparatus in Kosovo by the SFRY authorities and the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can speak of the bodies of the Federation and Serbia as taking over responsibility for the situation in Kosovo after mid-1990 when the process of disintegration of Yugoslavia began and when the separatist movement in Kosovo began changing into a national movement. There was an attempt made to paralyse the entire system including education, health care, economy as a whole, by people leaving their jobs, deserting properties and because of the worsening inter-ethnic relations, which was the reason for the introduction of special interim measures which came about at a later point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, and when you speak just now of bodies of the Federation of Serbia taking over the responsibility for the situation in Kosovo after mid-1990, the responsibilities included the responsibilities for the security organs in Kosovo. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs in Kosovo pursuant to these conclusions had their own remit and the Executive Council pronounced a number of measures based on the conclusions of the 3rd of March. That responsibility existed for the provincial bodies until the period when they ceased to exist or function when the Assembly was dissolved as well as a number of other bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If I could just take you back to some aspects of your evidence earlier. You were giving us or telling us the circumstances in which the Kosovo parliament or Assembly was dissolved. Do you recall that on the 2nd of July, 1990, members of the Kosovo Assembly were prevented from entering the Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly ceased its work before that. I think Mr. Bozovic pronounced that. And the continuation of the Assembly work was expected. I presume this was in that interim period when the delegates could not sit without the speaker. That is why we had the occasion when the declaration was read out in front of the Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But the declaration --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at 65 ter 00904.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was the declaration read out before, two days before the Kosovo Albanian parliament or Assembly was dissolved? This is the constitutional declaration of Kosovo as an independent unit of the Yugoslav Federation of the 3rd of July, 1990. Can you read the document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it. Could we please zoom in though. Could you please put your question now but precisely. What is your question about this declaration?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we zoom out to the top where we could see the date. Firstly, was the declaration of independence that was read out, was that on or about the 3rd of July, 1990?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a lot of time but it is likely that it was read out then. As for what was published in the "Official Gazette" and concerning what the presiding of the session is reported as having said, this was an illegal act. The printing of this issue was an illegal act without the knowledge of the federal organs. The Assembly still had its president, deputy president, and Executive Council. This declaration was read out in front of the building signed by the president or the speaker and signed by the delegates in attendance which is highly unusual. This does not have the characteristics of an official state document. This was merely a manifestation of that movement which wanted to grow to become a national movement in order to create all the necessary preconditions which would eventually result in their right to cessation coming about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And it was read out on the steps of parliament because they were locked out of parliament?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly is presided over by the speaker. If there's only one Chamber, then there's one speaker only. When the Assembly is not in session, the delegates are not in the building. As far as I know, the speaker would not have allowed them to enter and read out a declaration such as this one which is is unconstitutional declaring a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And thereafter the Serbian Assembly formally suspended the Kosovo Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at that. P1497 [Realtime transcript read in error "497"]. Could we tender the declaration which is before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01583.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the exhibit number should be 01583.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is correct. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems to me that the number of this exhibit was entered incorrectly. It should have been 1497 as previously stated by the Prosecution, whereas here I see 49. I would kindly ask Mr. Stamp to tell us what the correct number is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you make out this? This is a law dissolving the Kosovo Assembly.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the 5th of July. Yes, the law on the dissolving of the Assembly. I think I've already provided a number of answers to some of the previous questions put by counsel concerning the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, you have. Just one question on this, do you you recall now that the sequence of events was that Kosovo Albanian Assembly men or Assembly members were locked out of the Assembly, then they read their declaration of independence, which you say is illegal, we accept that's your view of it, and then the Serbian Assembly officially dissolved the Kosovo Assembly? Is that the sequence of how things occur?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the sequence and the dates in question, this jogs my memory. You are correct. First there were problems in the Kosovo Assembly and the Assembly could no longer resume its work normally because there had been attempts to read out the declaration inside the building during the session, but the other delegates would not have it. There was some discussion and arguments among the delegates, and the speaker called the session off. That's why the group of delegates in favour, probably on the next day, read it out at the entrance of the Kosovo Assembly building. What follows is Bozovic and the group of delegates going to Belgrade, then they returned, a conclusion was made that the Assembly could no longer sit, and it was dissolved. The Republic of Serbia, as the state of which Kosovo was a part of, tried to defend its territorial integrity in sovereignty by virture of these measures and would not have parts of its territory carved out illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Just could you assist us with the translation of Article 2 of this law on the termination by reading it out fully for us. Just read it slowly so we could get a translation for the record.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope you can hear me well. Article 2: "The rights and duties of the Assembly of the SAP Kosovo are being taken over by the Assembly of the SR Serbia and the Executive Council of the Assembly of the SAP Kosovo. The Executive Council of the Assembly of the SR Serbia until such time that a new Assembly of the SAP Kosovo and Executive Council are formed." This is Article 2 adopted by the Serbian Assembly in June. Article 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: July 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mentioned also that this declaration of independence was declared invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at another document. 01870 is the 65 ter number. Could we go to page 2 of the English. I believe, Your Honours, we should remove page 1 from the record. That relates to the proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you moving that that should occur?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Well, it's not yet in evidence, but in due course I think the proper thing would be to remove the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a decision on the constitutional declaration of the independence of Kosovo. If you look at item 1 we'll see what the constitutional court of Serbia was concerned with. And if we could move on to the decision on page 4. 4 in English and it's the last page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The decision was to quash the declaration. Yes, is that the decision that you spoke of earlier?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the decision of the constitutional court of Yugoslavia, not of Serbia as you have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this decision was put on the agenda by the constitutional court of Yugoslavia on its own initiative, and they declared that it was unconstitutional. This declaration was unconstitutional because the right to secession and self-determination was given only to republics and nations, not to provinces and nationalities. So basically the court confirmed what I said here and thereby the decision of the constitutional court declared this other declaration to be unconstitutional. When one reads it, one can see that in its form and in its content, it is not a legally valid document. It was a decision to voice their desires and goals. That's what that document was, it wasn't something based on the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is fine. The page in English is the correct one, but the page in Serbian does not correspond to the English one. But now give than the witness has said what he has said, the document itself doesn't matter. We should be showing the left side of the document, not the right side. It's good now. Could you now scroll up. This is something else. This is something concerning the Criminal Code. Yes, this is what we want to see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President of the constitutional court Milovan Buzadzic, yes, he was the president of the constitutional court of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could this document also be receive in evidence without this first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Without the first page. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01584.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could turn now, Mr. Jokanovic, to discuss briefly those amendments of the March 1989. I think it was the 29th of March, 1989. Prior those amendments, Kosovo Assembly had the power to veto constitutional change that the Serbian Assembly might propose. Is that your understanding of the situation?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. In that period of time, the Republic of Serbia did not have one of the basic constitutional responsibilities which was to create constitutions because the Assembly of Kosovo could have vetoed any amendment of the constitution of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that was one of the main grievances that many people had in respect to the 1974 constitution, the 1974 SFRY constitution?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the main complaints, but not the only one by no means. There were others. Other complaints concerning the defence system, state security, and typical functions of a state which any state in the world needs to have. The Republic of Serbia was a state yet it did not have some of those standard state functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P6. Document P6. The constitution of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, is it true, Mr. Jokanovic, that as a result of this amendment, an amendment that took away the right of the Kosovo Albanian Assembly to veto constitutional changes or changes with Serbian constitution, this constitutional amendment or this constitution was passed in September 1990?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of March, 1999 is when the constitutional amendments were adopted, and when it comes to amending the constitution, it involves a very complicated procedure. As for the constitution in 1990, it was a completely new constitution which introduced a multi-party system, which was a new democratic system that represented a discontinuation from the old communist regime. So they introduced a multi-party system and they also adopted various solutions in accordance with European standards and solutions that exist in some other European constitutions. This constitution is -- something is a cross between the French and the German constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. When this new constitution of 1990 was promulgated, could the Kosovo Albanian Assembly veto it?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the Kosovo Assembly nor the Vojvodina Assembly could have vetoed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They had lost that power as a result of the amendments in 1989? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They lost the right to veto. The Republic of Serbia once again could create its own constitution and a new complex procedure was established aimed at trying to find a harmonised solution, and if that did not succeed within a period of six months, then they could schedule a referendum, so they chose a solution whereby a referendum would replace a stalemate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did they -- my next question, Mr. Jokanovic, is did the 1990 constitution further restrict the limited autonomy that was being exercised by the -- exercised by the Kosovo Albanians, but I see it's time for the break, so I will ask that question again when we resume. Your Honours, I wonder if it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, we'll have the first break now and resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic. You looked as though you were coming to your feet, I thought you had another point. Mr. Stamp, Mr. Djurdjic was wanting to upstage you once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I realise it couldn't be a matter of you mistaking me for him, must have been otherwise. Thank you very much, Your Honours, I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, this is the constitution of Serbia, the Republic of Serbia of September 1990. Just to orient ourselves, could we look at Article 73, which is the general provisions with regard to the powers of the Serbian National Assembly. It will come up on the screen. I'm not sure if there's one in your binder. Mr. Jokanovic, it's being shown on the screen, on the screen in front of you. Article 73.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The general overarching powers of the national Assembly are set out there. You recall particularly articles 1 and 2 -- items 1 and 2 of that article? It had the power to decide on the constitution and to adopt laws and other regulations and general enactments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move to Article 109 in respect to the powers of the Kosovo and Metohija autonomous province.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you make it out now.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could please zoom in, I have a hard time seeing. These are the powers of the autonomous province which is to say that this constitution maintains the old system, mainly where Serbia has two province, Kosovo and Vojvodina. In Article 109 establishes the powers of autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at item 4.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This item speaks of implementation of laws, other regulations, and general enactments of the Republic of Serbia, whose implementation has been entrusted to the organs of autonomous province and it also adopts regulations on implementation of this legislation whenever specified so by law, which means that the law needs to be checked to see when it is that the organs are to implement laws in the territory of the entire republic and the province. This means that based on this article, they were to adopt a law specifying when the situations in which republic organs are to implement the laws in the territory of the entire republic including the province.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you look at Article 110. It's right there in the English.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said in my examination-in-chief, the status of the province changed over time so that from 1945 until 1963, the highest legal act was the statute and then they had the constitutional law and then the constitution. In 1974 they were granted the constitution. This new constitution introducing multi-party system, this new democratic constitution envisages once again that the highest enactment within the province is once again the statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in all of these provisions, the statute-making powers of the Kosovo Albanian is made subject to the authority of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which article do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see Article 10 there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean 110?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 110, thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And do you mean the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the second paragraph thereof, which is at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The highest legal enactment is this statute adopted by the autonomous province and its Assembly based on the prior approval of the national Assembly, they are referring to the National Assembly of Serbia, which is to say that the National Assembly of Serbia needs to give its consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it correct that the effect of these provisions that I've just shown you was to restrict or limit the authority of the Kosovo Assembly which it had previously processed before the amendment of 1989?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that the entire system was changed. Prior to this we had a socialist system based on self-management and delegate system, whereas now we had something similar to the system elsewhere in Europe, in other European countries. So if you look at the constitution from 1974 and this constitution, this put provinces in a different position. Pursuant to this constitution, the province had the so-called territorial autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, but what I'm asking you is this, isn't the effect of these provisions, the two provisions that I showed you, isn't it one of limiting the authority which is the Kosovo Assembly previously possessed?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this entirely new system and in these entirely new circumstances, in this new multi-party political system, if we were to compare this to the previous socialist system, then, yes, the province now had an entirely different status, and it was a restricted status.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we go to Articles 125, and I'm just interested in item 1, if we could look quickly at that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please enlarge this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Here we can see what was the authority of the constitutional court of Serbia. That's Article 125, item 1, "the constitutional court shall rule on conformity of law then statutes of autonomous provinces, other regulations and general enactments with the constitution."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could look at Article 30 [sic] now and then I'll ask the question. Sorry, 130, Article 130. Quite correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could, please, before the question.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So here we can see what is the jurisdiction of the constitutional court of Serbia, and this is to establish whether a law, we are talking about the laws of the republic or statute of autonomous provinces, were in line with the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, which means that the statute of an autonomous province, if it was contrary to the Serbian constitution and if this was thus established by the constitutional court, then probably the constitutional court would determine that the particular provision of this statute was unlawful or unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, prior to this constitution being promulgated in 1990, did the constitutional court of Serbia have the authority to decide upon the laws, the constitutional -- well, the laws of the autonomous provinces, in particular Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I will repeat that this was an entirely new social and political system, and it is rather difficult to compare this new multi-party system with the system as we had it after 1974. But if we were to compare it, then this could not be done pursuant to the 1974 constitution because at that time provinces had their own constitutional courts, so they had nearly all the authorities of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, as a matter of fact, by December 1990 the Serbian Assembly effectively abolished the Kosovo constitutional court?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to P20.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall that, Mr. Jokanovic? That the Serbian Assembly after passing this constitution giving them the power to adjudicate over the constitutional, over the laws of Kosovo and Metohija, they eventually abolished the constitutional court of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, in this new constitutional and political system of Serbia, there could not have been a constitutional court of Kosovo and Metohija because the constitutional court is established at the level of a state, and now this province, Kosovo and Metohija, had a status of a territorial autonomy, and as such it could not have a constitutional court. Whereas in line with the 1974 constitution, it did have a constitutional court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. And you recall that this decree before you, this is a decision relieving of duty the Judges of the Kosovo constitutional court, that was in December 1990?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given the provision that I just commented on a short while ago, this decision was made also to relieve of duty the judges of the constitutional court which existed according to the previous system and which now did not exist anymore, so this was a decision on relieving the Judges of the constitutional court of Kosovo of their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You testified earlier, Mr. Jokanovic, that when there was discussions on the proposed constitutional amendments in 1989, there was a significant amount of resistance by the Kosovo Albanians to these proposals. There were political protests, demonstrations, strikes. Would I be correct in saying that at that time in 1989, these proposed amendments were not popular with the Kosovo Albanian population in general?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1989, the situation was somewhat different because in 1989 there was still a wish to keep Yugoslavia together and to keep this province within the Republic of Serbia and Yugoslavia. The system as it was at the time was such that a majority of Albanians was also in favour of it and therefore they voted for the amendments of the constitution. But after Yugoslavia was disintegrated --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm not asking you about a majority of the Albanians in the Assembly just yet. I'm asking you about the Albanian population in general. Wouldn't you agree with me that these strikes and these protests and demonstrations indicated that these proposed amendments were not popular with the general Albanian population in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to say that nobody made any surveys, any research into the popularity or the percentage of the population that was in favour or against the proposals. There were many speculations, many rumours around and attempts to pass these proposals. I can't agree that the majority of the Albanian population was against the proposal. However, at the time the separatist movement was already there and in time it turned into a much wider, much more serious nationalistic movement, and in 1989, we still believed that the Yugoslav League of Communists was going to stay, and at that time there was 100.000 members of the League of Communists in Kosovo who supported the system as we headed at the time and a great number of Albanians as well as Roma and other nationalities lived well under such system. However, the circumstances were changing, and this is why the wish to have a separate state grew.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You read part of the testimony of Mr. Ibrahim Rugova where he said that the delegates or the representatives of the Kosovo Albanian parliament or Assembly were put under great pressure to pass the amendments in March 1989, and I think you will agree with me that these amendments to some degree or to a considerable degree reduced some of the powers which that Assembly had before. Can you tell us why in those circumstances they would agree to reducing the authority that they had before?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitutional amendments simply included changes to the provisions stipulating some of the state functions, whereas the position of the province within the Federation within Yugoslavia remained the same, so they kept their status and they kept their authority to regulate all the issues and implement all the legislation at the level of the province. So they kept a high level of autonomy, and at the same time they remained a constitutional element within Yugoslavia. This solution was accepted by a large number of Albanians as well because all the 22 Municipal Assemblies approved the amendments, and in the Municipal Assemblies obviously there were delegates from particular Assemblies, all the political organisations also approved them, and this was the socialist Alliance, trade unions and so on and so and. So the delegate system was such that the delegates conveyed the opinions of their constituents and they voted in line with the decisions passed by their constituents in their Assemblies. They were bound by such decisions. The same was done by the League of Communists and members of the League of Communists had to act in a given way. At that time the League of Communists was still stable and powerful, there was the provincial committee, and as he told you at that time in Kosovo there were 100.000 members of the league of communists and the largest number of the Assembly delegates were also members of the League of Communists. So based on the principle of democratic centralism, they were bound by the decision of the central committee of the League of Communists and the Executive Council of Kosovo, so as members of the communist league they were obliged to vote in the way in with which they did. We describe this system as a democratic centralism. Now, we could discuss how a system could be both democratic and centralised at the same way, at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You agree with what Mr. Rugova said that within the context that these Assembly members were put in, they were put under great pressure to vote as they did, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that they were pressured. I obviously understand while Mr. Rugova said what he did because he believed that Kosovo what supposed to secede and to become an independent state. This was his position as a member of the democratic Alliance of Kosovo. And obviously his intention was to make sure that what was happening in Slovenia and Croatia happened in Kosovo as well, but this was constitutionally impossible, and this is why he tried to use different illegal actions to raise Kosovo to the level of a republic, and we saw that illegal document that was signed by delegates, so this was simply an attempt to create preconditions for what was to follow. So they simply copied the situations in Slovenia and Croatia with referendums and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at 06096 quickly. 65 ter 06096.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a transcript of a BBC report of the 6th of February, 1991. And it says that: "Vukasin Jokanovic, vice president of the Serbian Assembly on the 4th of February, during talks with a group of primary school teachers from Pec stressed that due to the situation and dedication system in the province, many new measures would be introduced shortly in addition to the reduction in the amount of teaching Albanian. School headmasters will be given wider powers to enable them to carry out their duties more freely." The question is do you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I cannot recall this statement, that this statement is rather different from my entire political engagement and a number of other statements I gave. So I am not sure who conveyed this statement and how they did it, so I believe this is an example of propaganda. Because my name was -- carried certain weight, and at that time if these words were put into my mouth, this would imply that I supported the trends which went into direction of establishing Kosovo as a state and jeopardising Albanian population there, and I never ever with any statements of mine questioned the quality of Albanian population. And you can find thousands of my statements to that effect. My son searched the net and he found three or four hundred of my statements to this effect. So I can't recall this statement, and I believe it is false. I believe it was something that was put into my mouth, apparently there was an interview and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have your answer, I have your answer, Mr. Jokanovic. We just saw it and thought we'd give you an opportunity to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, I have nothing further for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, first of all, could we have P1469. There's no need for you to look through the binder. Please look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What we are about to see on the screen is the law on the work of republican organs under special circumstances together with the decree on the promulgation of such measures. It is P1469. What we have here. So P. I believe Mr. Stamp used it just a moment ago. This is not the document, Witness.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had to see it for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1496. Apologies. Could we now see ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This was published in the "Official Gazette" on the 26th of June, 1990. In Article 1 before the decree, what was the basis for the promulgation of this?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. There is a decree preceding this.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pursuant to Amendment 49, item 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it really 49? Or 39 perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 39. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What does it say then?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to Amendment 39, item 7 of the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia, this decree shall be put into force on the promulgation of the law on the work of republican organs under special circumstances by the various bodies of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where does it say that, Mr. Jokanovic?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does it say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to it, but please look at Article 2 of the law, so Article 2, item 1?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 2, item 1 states when special circumstances come into effect. In item 1 it says, Activities directed at overthrowing the constitutional order and the territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have items 2, 3, and 4 but let's not waste time. Please look at para 2 of Article 2, what does it stipulate?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia shall establish upon the proposal of the Executive Council of the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Serbia. Could you please show the bottom of the page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Actually, the right side of the page at the top. Centre it please. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That upon the proposal of the Executive Council of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, that special circumstances in a part of the republic have arisen or ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next could we please have Exhibit P71.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, this is a decision establishing that special circumstances have arisen in the territory of the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo. It came into effect on the 26th of June, 1999. It was published on that day the "Official Gazette" of Serbia. There is a figure there of 519, and what does it say just below that? What was the reason or the basis on which this decision was made?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to Article 2 of the law on the work of republican organs in special circumstances and Article 120 of the rules, the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia at the session of the council of associated labour on the 26th of June issued the decision establishing that special circumstances have arisen in the territory of the socialist autonomous province of Kosovo, meaning that precisely the circumstances I referred to before had arisen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was this decision based on?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 2 of the law on the work of republican organs in special circumstances, in brackets, the "Official Gazette" of the Republic of Serbia issued 30/90.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is this the law we just saw?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Certainly the decision was a result of that law. It could not stand on its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the decision of the SFRY Presidency on the introduction of special measures in Kosovo and Metohija made?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early March 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit P1583.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is the so-called constitutional declaration published in the "Official Gazette" of the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo in the 3rd of July, 1990. First of all, Mr. Jokanovic, we see here a list of those who signed allegedly the list, the declaration. Did you ever see the original list and the signatures of any of the people mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never did. It would be highly unusual to have people sign a certain piece of legislation, or enactment. Throughout my career I have never seen such an instance of people's names being published in the "Official Gazette" that way. As to whether they indeed signed it is a matter of further research or investigation, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear of a person presiding over a session?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in cases when a new Assembly is being established and then there is a presiding officer standing in for the speaker, but his sole authority is to declare that there will be a vote for the election of Assembly officials. Such a presiding officer neither according to the rules nor according to the constitution does not exist during the process of Assembly establishment. It is usually the most senior member who can preside during such a session. May I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the list followed by the abbreviations which stands for my own signature, I see a number of people who participated in or contributed to the session of the 23rd of March 1989, and there they voiced their support for the amendments. Whereas here, they seem to be signing a declaration proclaiming Kosovo an independent state, and this act even refers to the constitution of the SFRY calling the SFRY a confederation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 2 now. Please zoom in on the middle of the page. Yes, please go down a bit where it says "contents".

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It says here, Contents, probably of this issue of the "Official Gazette". Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This "Official Gazette" was published illegally. Seldom is an "Official Gazette" published with a single item. In the contents, we see that there is a reference made of Yugoslavia as a confederation and a federation. As the declaration says, this is what they refer to Yugoslavia, but I don't know where they invoke or on the basis of what they invoke this right to declare Yugoslavia a confederation, because at that time it was still an SFRY, a federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to P1497 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is the law on the secession of work of the Assembly of the Autonomous Province in Kosovo and the Executive Council of the Assembly of Kosovo published on the 5th of July, 1990. Could you please comment on Article 1 of the law.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to this article before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do not read it out loud, just comment.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, the Assembly of Kosovo had not been operational because they tried to undermine the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the country. It is also stated here that their work was directed against the constitutional system and the Republic of Serbia as a whole. It also states that the territorial integrity of Serbia is being brought into question so as to carve out a piece of its territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have P1584.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What we have now is the decision to assess the constitutionality of the constitutional declaration of Kosovo as an independent and equal unit within the framework of the Federation (confederation) of Yugoslavia as an entity equal to other units in the Federation (confederation). This was a decision of which constitutional court?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav constitutional court. Here we see the name of Milovan Buzadzic who was the president of the constitutional court of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to item 1, who initiated this procedure to assess the constitutionality of the declaration?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitutional court itself. It had the right to do things upon its own initiative or following proposals made by certain bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
