utterances.text: Thank you, I won't go through the whole decision, but I want to see the penultimate paragraph. This is it. Yes. Can you comment briefly. What did the constitutional court ascertain?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So as not to read the whole thing, the constitutional court concluded that the declaration was contrary to the constitution of Yugoslavia and that the provinces did not have such a right, only the republics did as states. This also applies to nations alone rather than nationalities. Nationalities could not make such declarations and proclaiming the province a republic serves to exclude its territory from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The reasons are stated here as well as what violations of the constitution of Serbia were made by way of this declaration. And I would like to ask you, Mr. Jokanovic, who took part in adopting this decision? Where were these judges of the constitutional court from?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milovan Buzadzic, Hervoje Barcic [phoen]. They were all from other republics, from Croatia, from Bosnia. Bozidar Bulatovic, by name I would say he was from Montenegro. Omer Ibrahimagic was a Muslim from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Branislav Ivanovic was most likely from Serbia. Pjeter Kola was from Kosovo. I know him, he was an eminent lawyer. Kapraroff [phoen] was probably a Hungarian. Vejlko Markovic was from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, what was the ethnicity of Pjeter Kola?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pjeter Kola was an Albanian from Kosovo and Metohija, and he held various offices in Kosovo and Metohija. Mostly administrative bodies and also legal positions similar to the positions that I held.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these judges from all republics and provinces of Yugoslavia, the Judges who adopted this decision?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how the constitutional court was organised in its composition. They had judges from all republics and provinces within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that in the constitution of 1990 a new multi-party system was introduced, and I would like to know whether the Albanian political parties that were established in accordance with this constitution took part in the political life in Serbia and whether they also participated in the elections?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanian parties did not take part in those elections. I know that one political party was registered and there were also others, and none of them participated because the participation in those elections would be contrary to their separatist and nationalist platform and programme which later developed its military side. Therefore, they boycotted the elections. However, not all of the Albanians participated in this boycott because some of the Albanians were on the ballots of some of political parties. On the ballot of the socialist party there were four Albanians, and they were elected to the new republic Assembly as delegates. I remember the names of some of them even. And they worked and took part in the work of the republic Assembly. They took part in adopting all of these enactments that we have mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This constitution, did it regulate the status of provinces within the Republic of Serbia in the identical way?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While following this trial on television, I heard many witnesses saying that the province was annulled, voided, which is not true. That's not what the constitution said. There was a province called Vojvodina and a province called Kosovo. Vojvodina had all of its organs, it had its Assembly, its Executive Council, and all of the other organs envisaged in the constitution. Whereas, Kosovo did not avail it itself of that right. They had a right to be represented in the Assembly of Serbia by many delegates. They chose not to do that. They didn't also want to establish a provincial Assembly because they thought that by doing so they would endanger their main goal, which was to have Kosovo established as a separate state and to have it secede from Serbia [Realtime transcript read in error "Kosovo"] and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we spoke about the amendments to the constitution of Serbia from 1989 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 15, it should read "to secede from Serbia and Yugoslavia," not from Kosovo and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to the transcript now? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When speaking of the 1989 amendments to the constitution of Serbia, and the right to veto, or rather, the inability to amend the constitution of Serbia without a prior consent of autonomous provinces, tell me, please, whether the Republic of Serbia could give its consent to the amendments of the provincial constitutions?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia and the Assembly of Serbia could neither consent or affect in any way the adoption of the Kosovo constitution. According to its constitution, Kosovo was fully independent to adopt its own constitution and in that regard Serbia had no powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the constitutional court of Serbia have the power to evaluate the constitutionality of the provisions of the Kosovo constitution to see whether it was in accordance with the federal constitution?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitutional court of Yugoslavia could assess, could evaluate whether certain provisions of the republic or provincial constitutions were in accordance with the federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, by way of these constitutional amendments which were adopted, or rather, to which they received a consent, what mechanism was there to amend the constitution of Serbia without the consent of the provinces?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a special amendment envisaging a complex procedure that would replace the right to veto. Once the Assembly of Serbia determined the text of the amendment, they would try to obtain a consent from provincial Assemblies. If they did not manage to obtain that consent then a parity based committee with representatives from Kosovo, Vojvodina, and Serbia would be established, and they would attempt to find a consensus, and then the adoption of that new amendment or that new constitution would be postponed by six months. If within these six months they failed to reach a consensus for a certain amendment, then the Assembly of Serbia could adopt that amendment after organising a referendum in which all citizens holding a right to vote would participate casting their votes. So that means that before those amendments would be adopted, there needed to be a referendum, and this is this complex procedure for circumventing the veto that I told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This referendum, did all citizens of the Republic of Serbia with a right to vote could participate in it?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of the voting citizens of the Republic of Serbia could participate including those living in provinces in Vojvodina and Kosovo, and naturally those living in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, could we now see P8, please. Could we now see Amendment 39, which should be page 25. I meant to say Amendment 29, I apologise, 29 not 39. In your binder that's tab 7 and pages 318 at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 318, Amendment 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Would you please take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you now give us a brief comment, please, of this amendment, when it comes to the assessment of whether the provincial constitution is in accordance with the constitution of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the provincial constitution contradicts the constitution of Serbia, then the constitutional court of Serbia would evaluate that and provide its opinion first to the Assembly of Serbia and then based on that opinion, the Assembly of Serbia, if it should establish that those provisions were in contradiction of the Serbian constitution could not void them immediately, but would inform the provincial Assembly of it giving them a one year dead-line to remove this contradiction. If the provinces fail to remove the contradiction within that period of time, then those provisions would not be implemented, would not be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I've no further questions for witness Jokanovic. Thank you, I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something for clarification. On Friday you spoke about and told us about a visit of a delegation of a European institution, and it is recorded as parliamentary delegation of the council, there's a word missing, council of Europe, I think. Today you spoke about I received the European parliament delegation. These are, I think, two different bodies. Was it a delegation of the parliamentary Assembly of the council of Europe or of the European parliament just for clarification?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was a delegation of the European parliament. So it was a parliamentary delegation of the council of Europe, that's how it was. Parliamentary delegation of the council of Europe. So a parliament was visiting a parliament of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, and the council of Europe was a body and European institution in which the socialist -- the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a member of, the European parliament is only comprising the member states of the European Union, that means that was a parliamentary Assembly of the council of Europe. That's correct, yes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember not being fully familiar with European institutions, I thought it was a parliamentary delegation of the European Union. I think that's how I remember it, but I could go over my documents to refresh my memory as to its formal name. It's been 30 years since then. At any rate, they came from a European institution and they were called a parliamentary delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, that completes the questions for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague and for the assistance that you have been able to give. You are, of course, now able to return to your normal activities. When we rise a Court Officer will show you out. Once again, thank you. We will now adjourn and resume with the next witness at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please read aloud the affirmation shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, sir. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mircic.

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mircic, before I ask with my questioning. First of all, I would kindly ask you since both of us speak the same language, once you've heard my question could you please wait for a moment so that the interpreters are allowed to do their job properly?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mircic, could you first of all state your name.

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: My name is Vukmir Mircic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When were you born?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 17th of September, 1958, in the village of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't catch the name of the village. Municipality of Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of village in which you were born?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Kodralija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mircic. Could you tell me if you were a member of the MUP and if so, since when?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've been a member of MUP since 1986. I worked in the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you still a member of MUP?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Well, now I'm -- I have been retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: I retired in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Could you please explain us briefly what were your duties within the Ministry of the Interior during your career?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: I was chief of the Decani department of Internal Affairs which belonged to the secretariat of MUP in Djakovica, and I was posted there on 1st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And prior to the 1st of January, 1993, what were your duties within the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: I was an inspector at the state security sector. And later on I was chief of detachment of the state security sector in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, during the course of 1998 and 1999 what was your position within the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: I was at that time still chief of the department for Internal Affairs of Decani, which belonged to the SUP of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what was the territory covered by your department of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: The Decani Department of Internal Affairs started -- let me start from the border with the Republic of Albania, so the border with Albania Montenegro, and then municipality of Pec and municipality of Djakovica. The length of the border with Albania was 22 kilometres, so the length of the border that belonged to the municipality of Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were your authorities as chief of the Department of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Well, my authorities were stipulated by all the laws and regulations adopted by the MUP. So the regulation on internal organisation and as chief I was tasked with monitoring the work of the police that fell under my jurisdiction, so the police station in which I had commander and assistant commanders who were in charge of the police stations within my Department of Internal Affairs. And the police station was also linked to the police department within the Secretariat of the Internal Affairs in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who was immediately superior to you in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 my directly superior was the chief of SUP of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1998 and 1999 did you receive all the orders exclusively from the chief of SUP of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the mixed commission for state border?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was appointed in 1996 by the federal SUP of Yugoslavia as a president of the LMK, which was local mixed commission for border, for the border in the sector 4th, which was the border with the Republic of Albania. And there were several members of this commission, usually five or six members of this commission was myself as president and then experts, some of them were members of the Army of Yugoslavia given that we were discussing the border and border-related issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us briefly what was the task of this mixed commission?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our task was to consider the incidents that occurred on either side of the border. If it occurred on the Albanian side, then they will notify us and obviously we considered this. If there was an incident on our side, we did the same. So all the border-related incidents, forest fires, illegal crossings, and different other incidents were considered jointly once a year both on our side and on their side of the border. So we had all the documents, we considered these incidents and passed relevant decisions. Decisions were whether we would register an incident, whether we would erase it from the register. If we couldn't agree, then the issue would be discussed by the second instance commission within the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What was the nature of your co-operation with the Albanian side with their mixed border commission, and how did you contact them?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Well, we would set a date and time for a meeting. I would go to the border crossing, usually Qafa Prushit [phoen], which was in the territory of the municipality of Djakovica, and as president of the commission I would go and meet their side there, so we exchanged letters and in this way a meeting was organised. They would come to our side with certain documents, and we would spend some time together and discuss all these incidents in order to try and establish the real truth concerning the incidents. The same was done on the Albanian side. So they also had teams which encompassed representatives on the police, the army, and other experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What was the nature of your co-operation?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Until 1998, I can say that it was correct, it was based on mutual respect, but often the Albanian side came with some really hard positions, so they had an input from an officer or somebody else, and they tried to convince us of that belief. But we also made quite a number of joint investigations. In 1996, 1997, even prior to those years, the border with Albania was -- the border between Albania and Yugoslavia made it possible for the terrorist groups and armaments to cross that border. And this is what happened after the regime in Albania changed when Salih Berisha came to power, so it was well known fact that there was anarchy in Albania. The arms were stolen from barracks and then they were smuggled to the territory of Kosovo. So the army tried to prevent such occurrences on a number of occasions, and they did prevent them and this is why we had several opportunities to carry out joint investigations. But because of rather complex security situation, we couldn't do this because the Albanian side opened fire to us. I warned their president of the commission on several occasions about this, about the incidents in the field, and he would tell me that he didn't know who fired. This was just a pretext with which they tried to prevent us from discovering the real situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mircic. Now that we are discussing these issues, could you please tell us what was the security situation in the territory of your OUP in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: In our estimate the security situation in the territory of the municipality of Decani was a very complex one. What made it more difficult was the arrival of terrorists to the territory of the municipality of Decani and also to the arrival of weapons. So in parallel, all the villages were armed. There were orders issued to certain persons to go to Albania and bring in weapons. Every village that was armed was signed in some way during the night. They would fire several times in order to inform the adjacent villages that they were armed, and I can also tell you that this is something that started to happen back in 1990s when I was still working for the state security sector. The terrorist groups were coming in. They were trained there in the town of Labinot, and on several occasions we discovered those illegal organisations and we also prosecuted them. I can also mention one terrorist attack in Decani itself carried out by Salih Ceka [phoen] which two other persons in a cafe where both Serbs and Albanians were coming, and on that occasion four or five civilians were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus on the year 1998 and 1999 now. This is what we are particularly interested in. Could you please tell us given the position of your Department of Internal Affairs, what was the security situation there?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: The security situation was very complex. My municipality was ethnically clean so to say so all the villages were Albanian, purely Albanian, particularly the villages next to the border. In my municipality I had approximately 700 Serbs, very few of them in some villages and even if those villages, the Serbian houses were at large distance from one other, and 99.9 per cent of the population was Albanian. And in 1998 and 1999, the situation was just as I described it, and the Serbs and Montenegrins started to move out from this region much earlier after 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mircic. We will talk more about this when we see some documents, but now, first of all, I would like a Defence binder to be provided to you. The first binder obviously, if Your Honours will allow this, I would like to show you some documents and when you see the documents on the screen, I will also inform you where you can find them in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the Exhibit P357. Sorry, P5357.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is number 1 in your binder. Mr. Mircic, these are the rules on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 6 in B/C/S. This is Article 4. I assume that it is the same page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at Article 4. In Article 4 you can see that within the secretariat referred to in Article 3 of these rules, the former -- the following departments of the Internal Affairs are established, and then we can see here Decani in Djakovica. So is this the article that regulates the department of the interior in Decani?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are the rules on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at Article 5. This is page 8 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So here in Article 8 we can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This is page 7 in English and Article 5. For the sake of Their Honours and other participants in this trial, we have to take a look at Article 5 in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So it says, Department of the interior and police stations under Article 4 of these rules shall directly perform tasks relating to Internal Affairs on the territory of these municipalities. Could you please comment on this article?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: By virtue of this article, several departments are being charged in taking over security responsibilities in the municipalities mentioned therein, which is in keeping with the Law on the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to Article 36, page 34 in the Serbian and 31 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The subtitle -- have you found Article 36? The subtitle is "organisational units in the municipalities." And Article 36 we see a department of the interior is responsible for, and I won't go reading the whole article, but I just wanted your comment in terms of the tasks and duties of the departments of the interior?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: In the Article 36 it says that a department of the interior is there to provide security to citizens and property in the area of the municipality, as well as to protect law and order, process crimes, border issues are mentioned as well. So this article regulates the scope of authority per departments concerning their work in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 2, it is stated that a department of interior consists of a police station. Within your OUP was there a police station?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mircic, please approach the microphone given that the interpreters can hardly hear you. Thank you. Within your OUP, were there any police detachments?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were two. In Ursnic [phoen] and Junik.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 48, please. I believe it is page 39 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Article 48. Yes, briefly only. Article 48 describes the scope of work of police stations. In the last of paragraph it is stated that police stations may include police branch stations or substations.

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it prescribes that there may be branch stations within OUPs and below police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So police substations as part of police stations?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, as part of OUPs and the police stations within the OUP of Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the tasks and duties from the interior domain which you performed as part of the OUP?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: That was stipulated by way of our internal organisation as per rules. We were supposed to work on crime prevention, preserving law and order, protect property and safety, property and citizens, administrative affairs, issuing of personal documents, driving licences, weapons, permits, and licences. Everything mentioned in the rules of the work of interior organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also perform duties which fell within the domain of regular police task, routine tasks?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to ask you yet again to pause before answering. Did you during 1998 and 1999 take part in the performing of special security related tasks in the area of Kosovo and Metohija? When I say you, I mean you as the chief of the OUP and your OUP as such?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How was the work of your OUP organised in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: As with other routine tasks before that period, i.e., protecting property, citizens, providing security, issuing IDs, drivers licences, administrative affairs, traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You've already said this, but I had in mind the way the OUP was organised.

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: The same as other routine, regular tasks and situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How many members did your OUP have?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: According to the structure, there should have been 117 [as interpreted] employees with the P status, meaning uniformed personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say 111?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Something else was recorded.

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: But we were never able to reach that figure so the most we had was about 80 P status personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within your OUP, were there any reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How and when were they engaged?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Members of the reserve force were usually engaged by order of the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P66.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 2. Mr. Mircic, this is the Law on the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]Could we see Article 28, please. In the English it's page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Article 28, first paragraph. Can you read it and tell us, please, whether it stipulates who and under what conditions can call on reserve police force members?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: It says, The minister may call up the members of the Ministry of the Interior as a reserve force to perform certain peacetime duties of the ministry, in particular to prevent activities aimed at threatening the security of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There's no need to read it all. We can see it for ourselves. Was it foreseen under this article --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Did this article prescribe how reserve police forces could be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it states that it should happen pursuant to the minister's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D102, it is your tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order to call up and engage reserve forces personnel to carry out certain peacetime tasks of the ministry. First of all, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: I do. From a collegium meeting with the chief of the secretariat. He acquainted us with this order based on the law of the interior on Article 28 on the call-up of reserve police members in order to complete certain tasks on behalf of the ministry. And this order prescribes the mode of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please go to item 5. Comment briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak out and approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every six months such orders were put in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please approach the microphone so that the interpreters can hear you. Very well. Could we next have D103.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 4.

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Briefly only, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a similar order to the previous one except that the date is the 1st of January, 1999, which means that such orders came into being every six months or so, as I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next could we please have D101.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 5. Instruction on or directive on the performance of Internal Affairs duties by reserve forces personnel of the ministry. Comment briefly, please. It was issued by Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic, the minister?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, this directive follows from the minister's order. It contains basic provisions. First it regulates the performance of duties and the way of reporting and informing per each and every item that needed to be acted upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw certain documents which serve as the basis for call-up of reserve police force members. In your OUP area what was the situation like and what need did you have for any reserve forces and were they engaged as part of your OUP?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Given the number of population in the municipality of Decani, I had very few reserve members who were engaged in routine tasks alongside active-duty policemen in patrols, on the beat, and at check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any specific circumstances concerning the engagement of reserve members and their serving alongside active-duty members?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: The reserve force could never set about a task independently. There were always to be accompanied by an active duty policemen, usually it would be the chief of a sector or the head of a patrol. Reservists could never independently perform tasks, and they were not trained to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within your OUP you said you had substations. Can you tell us where they were located?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: In the village of Ursnic and Junik.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who established these substations and how were they organised?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: As we said already, the minister issued a decision on internal organisation of these substations. Within their respective areas they had sectors for the performance of their tasks. They performed sectoral work in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P257.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 6. But before that, could you please tell us whether as part of your OUP you ever had any members of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How many such PJP members were there in your OUP?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Within my OUP there were usually at the level of one platoon, meaning 20 to 30 men strong headed by the platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which company did those PJP members belong to?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: To the SUP -- to the Djakovica SUP company.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to put some general questions to you about PJP units. Do you know when those units were established and whether they were established for the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. I was informed by the chief of the secretariat. We regularly held staff meetings, collegiums, and in one of such meetings the chief of the secretariat informed his immediate subordinates that 124th Intervention Brigade was created by the minister by way of a decision issued by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, when you say chief of the secretariat, who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Chief Kovacevic in the Djakovica SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as for the decision that is on the screen, we will return to it later. I wanted to focus on some general matters. Do you know about PJPs, when they were established and whether they were established for the territory of the entire Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: I already said about when they were established. And yes, they were established for the territory of the entire Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Were those regular police units, or were they engaged as needed?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: They are not regular police units. They were engaged as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, members of PJP units, when they were not engaged within such units, what duties and tasks did they perform?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: They performed regular routine duties and tasks just like all other police members.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know that PJPs in the 1990s, but before 1998 and 1999 were used in the territory of the Republic of Serbia, and if you do have such information, then tell us when?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: They were used in mass demonstrations, which were held in Serbia and primarily in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, I would like us to focus on PJPs within your OUP. How did you assemble and deploy members of PJPs, to be more precise, based on whose orders were they assembled and where were they sent?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Given that the minister adopted the decision on creating PJPs, it was done on the basis of his order. And then also based on the regional secretariat who within their line of work would send it to relevant OUPs. We would be informed either by dispatch or by phone that we needed to assemble a PJP with certain uniforms, with certain resources, and that we needed to deploy them to where they needed to be added to the Djakovica SUP company. The station commander was immediately in charge of that. He would convey this to the platoon commander. The platoon that belonged to the Decani OUP, and this is how they were organised. I would always be informed of their engagement and deployment -- deployment of the members of the PJP Decani OUP had who were within the composition of the Djakovica SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship between members of PJP who came from your organisation to you from the moment they were deployed?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: They had no responsibility vis-a-vis me. Either disciplinary nor any other. They were subordinated to their company commanders. They were already under the command of people who headed those companies and detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any reports about members of PJP who were originally from your OUP after their deployment?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: We would receive such reports in exceptional circumstances. If they were wounded out in the field or killed, so if there were any victims among the members of PJP, and if they were originally from our OUP, yes, we would be informed of such consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And were those the only reports you received in relation to members of PJP from your OUP?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were the only reports. No other reports.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up and speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to speak into the microphone. And to make a pause before answering my question. Mr. Mircic, did you you receive any sort of information about anti-terrorist actions or operations conducted by members of PJP units from your OUP?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: After deploying members of PJP, would you inform the police branch station within the secretariat on anything?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: That would normally be done by the commander of the substation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What would he inform them of?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: He would inform them about the composition of the unit, whether there were people who were absent, people who did not respond to a call-up, whether anybody was ill. Basically to inform them about the composition, about the strength of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And once that unit returned after completing their tasks and these members of PJP unit who were originally from your OUP, who would normally inform you about their imminent return and about when they needed to report to their regular duties?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: The chief of the police substation would inform with -- within his line of work, and I would also receive a copy of a dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mircic, thank you. Do you know who commanded forces of PJP units in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was the staff which was headquartered in Pristina. They were in command of PJP units in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who headed that staff?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Sreten Lukic was the head of that staff. General Lukic. The staff was established from two departments, state security department and public security department. Lukic's deputy was Gajic, David Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: He was deputy of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And he belonged to which department?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: To the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mircic, given that you first worked for the state security department and then for the public security department, tell us, please, whether the chief of the public security department could issue any sort of orders to the members of the state security department?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: No, out of the question. He could only issue his orders within his line of work, which was the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And who could then issue orders to this body which assembled together both members of the public security and state security department?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Lukic, General Lukic could.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who established this staff headed by General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes. That staff was created based on the decision of the minister of the interior of Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know of this?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: We were told of this in our regular meetings with the chief of the secretariat, collegium meetings. He informed us that the staff had been created and that chiefs of secretariats were members of the expanded composition of that staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion, did the chief of the secretariat tell you to whom the staff headed by Lukic was responsible?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, he told us. He told us that the staff headed by Lukic was directly responsible to the minister, Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mircic, did you visit your units, members of PJP from your OUP after they had been deployed?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: No, I never visited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, given that we have this decision on the screen, the decision on establishing the 124th Intervention Brigade of the PJP, tell us please, do you know of this decision?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it. It was read at one of our collegium meetings within the Djakovica SUP. We were informed of it as part of our regular duties. This is a decision number such and such, pursuant to which the 124th Intervention Brigade of PJPs was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were members of a PJP unit from your OUP deployed to the 124th Intervention Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, since they were members of the company of the Djakovica secretariat. They became members of the 124th Brigade because 124th Brigade was for the territory of the entire Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mircic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D008-0594, which is your tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mircic, this is a dispatch from the 13th of April, 1998 in which it says that: "We have intelligence that all men fit for military service from the village of Crnobreg, Decani municipality have been armed with standard issue weapons and artillery shipped illegally from Albania under the arrangements made by the DSK." Could you please comment on this, and does this reflect the security situation in the Decani area?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is just one of the pieces of information concerning the village of Crnobreg. All villages were armed, Albanians and terrorist groups were armed and established in each village.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 7 in the B/C/S version and in the English one as well. And as for my learned friend from the Prosecution and the Chamber, I will tell you that the same information is repeated on the pages in between, so I think it would be a waste of time if we were to spend much time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mircic, would you please look at page 7 and the document there. That is a dispatch dated 13th of April, 1998. And in the middle of that document they say: "We also have information that other terrorist groups are acquiring artillery guns as well. For example, a terrorist group in Jablanica has in their possession four guns which according to our information had been stolen from the Army of Yugoslavia in the area of Drenica." Did you have such information that KLA had this type of weaponry as well?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: All intelligence received from the ground indicated that they had both heavy weapons and small arms. They had recoilless guns, mortars, 112 millimetres and 60 millimetres. They had heavy machine-guns, 12 and 7. They had shoulder rocket-launchers. They had explosives and mines. They had the entire arsenal within the infantry weaponry and small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now turn to page 9 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mircic, again this is dispatch number 27. 13th of April, 1998. In the first paragraph they state --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the following page in the English version. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We have intelligence that: "On the 12th of April, 1998 in the village of Istinic in Decani municipality leaders of the DSK had a meeting with Siptar residents of the village of Istinic where a request was made for the villagers to arm themselves and for a terrorist group from Jablanica to be deployed in the village to defend it from the Serbian aggressor." Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, just like all the previous information, the village of Istinic belongs to the same group, in the vicinity of Decani. The main role was played by the staff headed by Ramush Haradinaj in the village of Jablancia. All the villages were barricaded with trenches surrounding them and protected by heavy weaponry that they had their place. Every village had a local commander and every village had establishment terrorist groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please turn to the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. Mircic, on the 12th of April, the following Serbian and Montenegrin families left their homes for security reasons, and then they go on to list the names of these families and the names of family members. Did you have any such information, can you tell us something briefly about it?

utterances.speaker: VUKMIR MIRCIC
utterances.text: Yes, the families that were in minority in those areas -- in those villages moved out. They came to Decani for their own personal safety. On the road to Decani terrorist groups would detain certain persons in the staff in the village of Glodjani from which Ramush Haradinaj hails and where his staff was. We had an eye-witness who had been released from that staff. He was a Montenegrin by origin and Haradinaj's father released Kostadin Stijovic [phoen]. He refused to lock him up, and this man came to me at the SUP and told me about everything that had happened, which is to say, that he had been released due to some friendly causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mircic, and before we break for today, could we have this document admitted into evidence, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00910.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must resume now for the evening. We resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. A Court Officer will assist you when we adjourn.
